title: Part 103 Ultralight Primer
note: Original OpenChecklists questions written from the text of 14 CFR Part 103. Not an FAA test: Part 103 requires no knowledge test.

questions.stem: What is the maximum empty weight of a powered ultralight vehicle under Part 103?

choices.A: Less than 254 pounds, excluding floats and emergency safety devices such as a ballistic parachute.
choices.B: Less than 254 pounds, including fuel and the pilot.

questions.explanation: A powered ultralight must weigh less than 254 pounds empty. Floats and safety devices intended for deployment in a potentially catastrophic situation are not counted. The 155-pound limit applies to unpowered ultralights.

questions.stem: What is the maximum fuel capacity of a powered ultralight vehicle?

choices.A: There is no fuel limit; only empty weight is limited.

questions.explanation: A powered ultralight may have a fuel capacity of no more than 5 U.S. gallons.

questions.stem: What is the maximum speed of a powered ultralight in level flight at full power?
questions.explanation: A powered ultralight must not be capable of more than 55 knots calibrated airspeed at full power in level flight. 87 knots is a light-sport aircraft figure, not a Part 103 limit.

questions.stem: What is the maximum power-off stall speed of a powered ultralight?
questions.explanation: The power-off stall speed of a Part 103 powered ultralight may not exceed 24 knots calibrated airspeed.

questions.stem: How many occupants may an ultralight vehicle carry?

choices.A: Two, if the second occupant is a flight instructor.
choices.C: Two, if both are wearing parachutes.

questions.explanation: By definition an ultralight is used or intended to be used for manned operation by a single occupant, for recreation or sport purposes only.

questions.stem: Which certificates does Part 103 require of an ultralight operator?

choices.A: A student pilot certificate and a third-class medical.
choices.B: A sport pilot certificate with an ultralight endorsement.

questions.explanation: Ultralight operators are not required to meet any aeronautical knowledge, age or experience requirements, or to hold airman or medical certificates. Training is still strongly recommended.

questions.stem: Must an ultralight vehicle be registered and carry an N-number?

choices.A: No. Ultralights are not required to be registered or to bear markings of any type.
choices.B: Yes, all aircraft operated in the United States must be registered.
choices.C: Only if it is flown in controlled airspace.

questions.explanation: Ultralight vehicles are not required to be registered or to bear markings of any type, and they do not need airworthiness certificates.

questions.stem: Without additional equipment, during what hours may an ultralight be operated?

choices.A: Any time, if the operator remains clear of clouds.
choices.C: From 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset.

questions.explanation: Ultralights may operate only between sunrise and sunset. The twilight periods are allowed only with additional equipment and only in uncontrolled airspace.

questions.stem: An ultralight may fly during the 30-minute twilight periods before sunrise and after sunset only if

choices.A: it has navigation lights and the operator has notified the nearest tower.
choices.B: the operator holds a private pilot certificate.
choices.C: it has an operating anticollision light visible for at least 3 statute miles and stays in uncontrolled airspace.

questions.explanation: Twilight operations (30 minutes before official sunrise and 30 minutes after official sunset) require an operating anticollision light visible for at least 3 statute miles, and all operations must be in uncontrolled airspace.

questions.stem: Who has the right-of-way when an ultralight meets another aircraft?

choices.A: The ultralight yields to all aircraft; a powered ultralight also yields to an unpowered ultralight.
choices.B: The ultralight, because it is the least maneuverable.

questions.explanation: Ultralight operators must see and avoid and yield the right-of-way to all aircraft. Powered ultralights must yield to unpowered ultralights.

questions.stem: Over which areas is ultralight operation prohibited?

choices.A: Over a congested area below 1,000 feet AGL only.
choices.B: Any congested area of a city, town or settlement, or any open-air assembly of persons.
choices.C: Only areas with more than 1,000 residents.

questions.explanation: Part 103 has no altitude exception: no person may operate an ultralight over any congested area of a city, town or settlement, or over any open-air assembly of persons.

questions.stem: What is required before operating an ultralight in Class B, C or D airspace, or in the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport?

choices.A: A transponder and two-way radio only.
choices.B: Nothing, if the flight remains below 500 feet AGL.
choices.C: Prior authorization from the ATC facility having jurisdiction over that airspace.

questions.explanation: Operations in Class A, B, C or D airspace, or within the lateral boundaries of a Class E surface area designated for an airport, require prior authorization from the ATC facility having jurisdiction.

questions.stem: When may an ultralight operate in a restricted or prohibited area?

choices.A: Only with permission from the using or controlling agency.
choices.B: Whenever the area is shown as inactive on the sectional chart.

questions.explanation: Ultralights may not operate in prohibited or restricted areas unless the operator has permission from the using or controlling agency.

questions.stem: Part 103 requires an ultralight to be operated

choices.A: at or below 500 feet AGL at all times.
choices.B: only by visual reference with the surface.
choices.C: with a GPS when beyond sight of the departure field.

questions.explanation: No person may operate an ultralight except by visual reference with the surface. There is no instrument flying in an ultralight.

questions.stem: What are the minimum flight visibility and cloud clearance for an ultralight in Class G airspace at 1,200 feet or less above the surface?

choices.A: 3 statute miles and 500 feet below the clouds.
choices.B: 5 statute miles and 1,000 feet above the clouds.
choices.C: 1 statute mile and clear of clouds.

questions.explanation: The Part 103 table sets 1 statute mile flight visibility and clear of clouds in Class G airspace at 1,200 feet or less above the surface, regardless of MSL altitude.

questions.stem: What are the ultralight visibility and cloud clearance minimums in Class E airspace below 10,000 feet MSL?

choices.A: 3 statute miles; 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.
choices.B: 1 statute mile and clear of clouds.
choices.C: 5 statute miles; 1,000 feet below and above, and 1 statute mile horizontally.

questions.explanation: Below 10,000 feet MSL in Class E, Part 103 requires 3 statute miles visibility and 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds.

questions.stem: May an object be dropped from an ultralight vehicle?

choices.A: Yes, at any time over unpopulated areas.
choices.B: Only if dropping it does not create a hazard to other persons or property.

questions.explanation: No person may allow an object to be dropped from an ultralight if doing so creates a hazard to other persons or property.
